items.stem: Think about how you decided whether an object was in motion or at rest. Write your explanation (justification) in Table. Table : Observing things around you Objects in motion Justification Objects at rest Justification Cow grazing in the field Tree
items.answer: To complete the activity:

items.stem: Observe its motion. Does it move along a straight line? When an orange drops from the tree, does it move in a straight line? Have you seen the Republic Day parade? Recall the march-past of students during the parade. Do they move on a straight-line path? When a heavy box is pushed, it may also move along a straight line (Figure). Figure : Linear motion
items.answer: 1. Yes, it moves along a straight line (vertically downwards).

items.stem: Observe its motion. Figure : Circular motion Is the motion of the eraser the same as that of a merry-go-round? When an object moves along a circular path, its motion is called circular motion.
items.answer: 1. Observation : When you hold the thread and whirl the eraser, you will observe that the eraser moves in a circle around your hand. Its path is circular.

items.stem: Using the other hand, take the eraser slightly to one side and then release (Figure). Does it start moving to and fro? Is its motion similar to the motion of a swing? When an object moves to and fro about some fixed position, its motion is called oscillatory motion. Figure : Oscillatory motion Observation : When you pull the hanging eraser to one side and release it, it does start moving to and fro. It swings back and forth repeatedly about its initial resting position (the lowest point).
items.answer: Yes, the motion of the swinging eraser is very similar to the motion of a child on a swing. Both exhibit a repeating back-and-forth movement around a central point. This setup (eraser on a thread) is a simple pendulum. Activity 5.6 : Let us investigate

items.stem: Observe the motion of this end of the strip. Does it move up and down? This is also an example of oscillatory motion. Observation : When you press the free end of the metal strip down and release it, you will observe that the end moves up and down rapidly, vibrating about its original horizontal position.
items.answer: Yes, the motion is up and down , this type of vibration (moving back and forth, or in this case, up and down, about a fixed equilibrium position) is indeed another example of oscillatory motion. Activity 5.7 : Let us identify

items.stem: Some lengths are given in Column I of Table. Some units are given in Column II. Match the lengths with the units suitable for measuring those lengths. Column I Column II Distance between Delhi and Lucknow centimetre Thickness of a coin kilometre Length of an eraser metre Length of school ground millimeter
items.answer: Column I Column II Distance between Delhi and Lucknow kilometre Thickness of a coin millimeter Length of an eraser centimeter Length of a school ground metre (i) Kilo metres (km) are used for long distances between cities. (ii) Millimeters (mm) are suitable for measuring very small thicknesses. (iii) Centimeters (cm) are convenient for small objects like erasers. (iv) Metres (m) are appropriate for larger lengths like playgrounds or rooms.

items.stem: Read the following statements and mark True (T) or False (F) against each. (i) The motion of a car moving on a straight road is an example of linear motion. [ ] (ii) Any object which is changing its position with respect to a reference point with time is said to be in motion. [ ] (iii) 1 km = 100 cm [ ]
items.answer: (i) T (True). Linear motion is defined as motion along a straight line. (ii) T (True). This is the definition of motion. (iii) F (False). 1 kilometre (km) = 1000 metres (m), and 1 metre (m) = 100 centimetres (cm). Therefore, 1 km = 1000 100 cm = 100,000 cm.

items.stem: Which of the following is not a standard unit of measuring length? (i) millimeter (ii) centimeter (iii) kilometre (iv) hands pan
items.answer: (iv) hands pan Millimeter, centimeter, and kilometre are standard units derived from the base SI unit of length, the metre. A hands pan is a non-standard unit because its length varies from person to person.

items.stem: Search for the different scales or measuring tapes at your home and school. Find out the smallest value that can be measured using each of these scales. Record your observations in a tabular form.
items.answer: This question requires performing an activity. The smallest value that can be measured is called the least count of the instrument. Procedure : Look at the markings on different scales (like a 15 cm ruler, a 30 cm ruler, a metre scale, a measuring tape). Find the value represented by the smallest division marked on the scale. Example: Observation Table:

items.stem: What was Deepa’s mother’s instruction to the tailor regarding the length of the new uniform?

options.label: A
options.text: To decrease the length by two fingers width

options.label: B
options.text: To increase the length by char angula (four fingers width)

options.label: C
options.text: To keep the length the same as the old uniform

options.label: D
options.text: To measure the length using a metal rod only

items.answer: (B) To increase the length by char angula (four fingers width). Deepa’s mother asked the tailor to lengthen her new uniform by char angula, meaning four fingers’ width—an example of a traditional unit of measurement.

items.stem: Why did Deepa and her friends get different measurements for the length of the same table when using their hands pans?

options.label: B
options.text: Some students did not know how to count properly

options.label: C
options.text: Their hands pans were of different sizes

options.label: D
options.text: They used different parts of their hands

items.answer: (C) Their hands pans were of different sizes. Using body parts like hands pans for measurement leads to varied results because the size of these body parts differs from person to person. This inconsistency highlights the need for standard units.

items.stem: What is the SI unit of length?
items.answer: (C) Metre The SI (International System of Units) standard unit for measuring length is the metre, represented by the symbol ‘m’, and it helps maintain consistency in measurements across the world.

items.stem: How many centimeters are there in one metre?
items.answer: (B) 100 centimeters A metre is divided into 100 equal divisions, and each of these divisions is called a centimetre. Therefore, 1 metre is equivalent to 100 centimeters.

items.stem: Why is it generally inconvenient to use the unit metre to measure very large distances, like between cities, or very small lengths, like the thickness of a page?

options.label: A
options.text: Metre scales are not accurate for any distance

options.label: B
options.text: The numbers involved become too large or too small, making them unwieldy

options.label: C
options.text: Metres can only be used for measuring cloth

options.label: D
options.text: The SI system does not allow using metres for such lengths

items.answer: (B) The numbers involved become too large or too small, making them unwieldy. For very large distances, expressing them in metres results in very large numbers, while for very small lengths, it results in very small decimal numbers. Larger units (like kilo metres) or smaller units (like millimetres) are more practical.

items.stem: What is the smallest value of length that can typically be measured using a standard 15-cm classroom scale?
items.answer: (C) 1 millimeter A standard 15-cm scale has each centimeter divided into 10 equal parts, where each part represents 1 millimetre. This is the smallest division, hence the smallest value accurately measurable.

items.stem: How many millimetres are there in one centimetre?
items.answer: (C) 10 millimetres (ii) The motion of a point on the blade of a spinning fan. (Other examples : Merry- go-round, stone whirled on a string)

items.answer: This requires observation. Here’s an example completion: Size Objects mm Thickness of a coin, Pencil lead diameter, Ant’s length cm Length of a pencil, Width of a book, Length of a mobile phone m Length of a room, Height of a door, Length of a blackboard

items.answer: 1. Portion A to B : The ball moves down a slope, mostly straight. This is primarily Linear motion (or motion along a straight line).

items.answer: Tasman should not use paper, cloth and stretchable rubber. Why:

items.answer: Let’s assume you measure your friend’s height and find it to be 145 centimeters.

Estimate how many coins are required to be placed one after the other lengthwise, without leaving any gap between them, to cover the whole length of the chosen side of a notebook. Verify your estimate by measuring the same side of the notebook and the size of the coin using a 15-cm scale.
items.answer: This involves estimation and measurement.

items.stem: Give two examples each for linear, circular and oscillatory motion.
items.answer: 1. Linear motion: (i) A car moving on a straight road. (ii) An apple falling from a tree. (Other examples : Athlete running on a straight track, train on a straight track)

items.stem: What is the main advantage of using standard units of measurement (like SI units) over traditional units (like hands pan or Angola)?

options.label: A
options.text: Standard units are easier to remember

options.label: B
options.text: Traditional units are more accurate for small lengths

options.label: C
options.text: Standard units ensure consistency and avoid differences in measurements made by different people

options.label: D
options.text: Traditional units do not require any measuring tools

items.answer: (C) Standard units ensure consistency and avoid differences in measurements made by different people. Traditional units based on body parts vary from person to person, leading to inconsistent measurements. Standard units provide a common, unchanging reference, ensuring uniformity and reliability in measurements globally.

items.stem: If a tailor needs to measure the girth of a tree or the size of a person’s chest, which measuring tool would be most suitable?
items.answer: (C) A flexible measuring tape. For measuring curved surfaces or circumferences like the girth of a tree or a person’s chest, a rigid scale is unsuitable. A flexible measuring tape can conform to the curve, providing an accurate measurement.

items.stem: What is the correct way to place a scale when measuring the length of an object?

options.label: A
options.text: Slightly above the object without touching it

options.label: B
options.text: At an angle to the object’s length

options.label: C
options.text: In contact with the object, along its length

options.label: D
options.text: With the zero mark always at the right end of the object

items.answer: (C) In contact with the object, along its length. To measure accurately, the scale should be placed directly in contact with the object being measured, and aligned parallel to the length that is to be measured.

items.stem: A student is measuring the length of a pencil using a scale whose zero mark is broken. The student aligns one end of the pencil with the 2.0 cm mark, and the other end aligns with the 11.5 cm mark. What is the actual length of the pencil?
items.answer: (C) 9.5 cm When the zero mark is unusable, one end of the object is aligned with another clear mark on the scale. The length is then found by subtracting this starting mark’s reading from the reading at the other end: . . . cm cm cm 11 5 2 0 9 5 - = .

items.stem: How do visually challenged students typically measure lengths?

options.label: A
options.text: By estimating the length based on sight

options.label: B
options.text: Using scales with raised markings that can be felt by touch

options.label: C
options.text: By having someone else measure for them

items.answer: (B) Using scales with raised markings that can be felt by touch. Visually challenged individuals use specially designed scales with raised, tactile markings that allow them to feel and understand measurements through touch..

items.stem: What is a reference point in the context of describing an object’s position or motion?

options.label: A
options.text: Any point chosen randomly in space

options.label: B
options.text: The object whose position is being described

options.label: C
options.text: A fixed object or point with respect to which position or motion is stated

options.label: D
options.text: The unit used to measure the distance

items.answer: (C) A fixed object or point with respect to which position or motion is stated. A reference point is a stationary location or object used for comparison to determine if something is moving or to describe its position accurately.

items.stem: Why did Deepa and her friends initially have different ideas about whether the garden or the school was closer?

options.label: A
options.text: Because the garden and school kept changing their locations

options.label: B
options.text: Because they were each considering the distance from their own houses (different reference points)

options.label: C
options.text: Because some of them were not good at judging distances

options.label: D
options.text: Because they were using different units of measurement

items.answer: (B) Because they were each considering the distance from their own houses (different reference points). Their perceptions of closer or farther differed because each was using their own house as the reference point. If they had used a common reference point, their observations of relative distances would have been consistent.

items.stem: Padma is on a bus trip to Delhi. She sees a kilometre stone that reads Delhi 70 km. Later, she sees one that reads Delhi 60 km. What is the reference point for these distances?

options.label: B
options.text: The bus she is travelling in

items.answer: (C) The city of Delhi. The kilometre stones indicate the remaining distance to Delhi. Therefore, Delhi is the fixed reference point against which Padma’s changing position (and distance) is being measured.

items.stem: When is an object said to be in motion?

options.label: B
options.text: When its position changes with respect to a reference point with time

options.label: C
options.text: When it changes its shape or size

options.label: D
options.text: When it is making a sound

items.answer: (B) When its position changes with respect to a reference point with time. Motion is defined as the change in an object’s position over time relative to a fixed reference point. If there’s no change in position relative to the reference point, the object is at rest.

items.stem: If Deepa is on a moving bus and considers herself as the reference point, are the other seated passengers in motion or at rest relative to her?

options.label: A
options.text: They are in motion because the bus is moving

options.label: B
options.text: They are at rest because their position is not changing relative to Deepa

options.label: C
options.text: Some are in motion and some are at rest

options.label: D
options.text: It’s impossible to tell without looking outside

items.answer: (B) They are at rest because their position is not changing relative to Deepa. Motion is relative. If Deepa (also on the bus) is the reference point, and the other passengers maintain their seated positions, their position relative to Deepa does not change with time, so they are at rest with respect to her.

items.stem: What type of motion is described when an object moves along a straight line?
items.answer: (C) Linear motion Linear motion, also known as rectilinear motion, is characterized by an object moving along a straight path or line. Examples include a car moving on a straight road or a dropped object falling vertically.

items.stem: What type of motion does a merry-go-round exhibit?
items.answer: (B) Circular motion A merry-go-round involves objects or people moving in a circular path around a central axis. This type of movement is defined as circular motion.

items.stem: What is oscillatory motion?

options.label: A
options.text: Motion in a perfect circle at a constant speed

options.label: B
options.text: Motion along a straight line without changing direction

options.label: C
options.text: Motion where an object moves to and fro about some fixed position

options.label: D
options.text: Motion that covers equal distances in equal intervals of time

items.answer: (C) Motion where an object moves to and fro about some fixed position. Oscillatory motion is a repetitive back-and- forth movement of an object around a central or equilibrium position. A swinging pendulum is a classic example.

items.stem: A child on a swing moves back and forth. What type of motion is this?
items.answer: (C) Oscillatory motion The movement of a child on a swing is a repetitive to-and-fro motion about a central, lowest point. This is a characteristic example of oscillatory motion.

items.stem: What does it mean if an object’s motion is periodic?

options.label: A
options.text: It moves only in a straight line

options.label: C
options.text: It repeats its path after a fixed interval of time

options.label: D
options.text: It covers a very long distance

items.answer: (C) It repeats its path after a fixed interval of time. Periodic motion is any motion that repeats itself in equal intervals of time. Both circular motion (like a planet orbiting) and oscillatory motion (like a pendulum) can be periodic.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of a unit of length mentioned in ancient Indian literature?
items.answer: (D) Fathom Ancient Indian texts refer to units of length such as angula, dhanusa, and yojana, while the fathom is a unit of length from another historical system, commonly used to measure water depth.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Measurements made using hands pans can vary from person to person. Reason (R) : The size of a person’s hands pan is not a universally fixed standard.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Hands pans differ in size among individuals. Because there’s no standard size for a hands pan, using it as a unit of measurement will inevitably lead to different numerical results for the same length when measured by different people.

items.stem: When reading a scale, your eye should be directly above the mark.
items.answer: (C) 1 and 3 only The SI unit of length is indeed the metre. For accurate reading, the eye position should be directly above the mark to avoid parallax error. A flexible tape or thread is better for curved lines than a rigid scale.

items.stem: A carpenter is building a bookshelf. To ensure the shelves are of the correct width, she uses a metal rod with markings on it. This metal rod is an example of a:
items.answer: (C) Measuring scale using standard units. A metal rod with centimeter and millimeter markings is a measuring scale that uses standard SI units (or their subdivisions) for length, ensuring accuracy and consistency in the carpenter’s work.

items.stem: What is the name of the system of units that is now used internationally for standard measurements?
items.answer: (B) The Metric System (specifically SI) The currently used system of measurement is called the ‘International System of Units’ or SI units, which is the modern version of the metric system.

items.stem: If you are measuring the length of a piece of cloth and the end of your metre scale is broken (the ‘0’ mark is missing), what should you do to get an accurate measurement?

options.label: A
options.text: Estimate the missing part and add it to the reading

options.label: B
options.text: Start measuring from any full mark (e.g., 1 cm or 10 cm) and subtract that starting value from the final reading

options.label: C
options.text: Use the broken end as if it were zero

options.label: D
options.text: The scale cannot be used accurately anymore

items.answer: (B) Start measuring from any full mark (e.g., 1 cm or 10 cm) and subtract that starting value from the final reading. If the zero mark is damaged, an accurate measurement can still be obtained by aligning one end of the object with another clear, full mark on the scale and then subtracting that mark’s value from the reading at the object’s other end.

items.stem: When an object moves along a circular path, its motion is called:
items.answer: (C) Rotational motion (or Circular motion) Motion that follows a circular path is known as circular motion, while rotational motion refers to an object spinning around its own axis—both are closely related types of movement..

items.stem: The traditional Indian unit of length angula refers to:
items.answer: (C) The width of a finger. Angula (finger width) was one of the units used in ancient Indian measurement systems.

items.stem: How does linear motion differ from circular motion?

options.label: A
options.text: Linear motion is always fast; circular motion is always slow

options.label: B
options.text: Linear motion is along a straight line; circular motion is along a curved, circular path

options.label: C
options.text: Linear motion involves repetition; circular motion does not

options.label: D
options.text: Linear motion requires a reference point; circular motion does not

items.answer: (B) Linear motion is along a straight line; circular motion is along a curved, circular path. The defining characteristic of linear motion is movement in a straight line. In contrast, circular motion involves an object moving along the circumference of a circle or a circular arc.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT a type of motion explicitly discussed with examples in section 5.7 Types of Motion?
items.answer: (D) Vibrational motion Section 5.7 focuses on illustrating linear, circular, and oscillatory motions with activities and examples. While vibrational motion is related to oscillatory, it is not explicitly detailed as a distinct category in this section.

items.stem: The hands of a clock moving around the dial primarily exhibit which type of motion?
items.answer: (B) Circular motion The tips of the hands of a clock trace circular paths as they move around the center of the clock face. This is a clear example of circular motion.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : An object can be at rest with respect to one reference point and in motion with respect to another. Reason (R) : Motion is a relative concept and depends on the chosen reference point.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The state of rest or motion of an object is not absolute but depends on the frame of reference. For instance, a passenger on a bus is at rest relative to the bus but in motion relative to the ground.

items.stem: A plucked guitar string.
items.answer: (B) 2 and 3 only A child on a swing and a plucked guitar string both exhibit to-and-fro movement about a central position, which is characteristic of oscillatory motion. A car on a straight highway undergoes linear motion.

items.stem: A teacher asks students to measure the length of their classroom using a 15-cm scale. Why would this be an inefficient method?

options.label: A
options.text: A 15-cm scale cannot measure lengths greater than 15 cm at all

options.label: B
options.text: It would require repeated measurements, increasing chances of error and taking a lot of time

options.label: C
options.text: Centimetres are not standard units for classroom length

options.label: D
options.text: The scale is too flexible for measuring a room

items.answer: (B) It would require repeated measurements, increasing chances of error and taking a lot of time. Using a very small measuring tool (15-cm scale) for a relatively large length (8 metres) necessitates laying the scale multiple times. This process is tedious, time-consuming and accumulates errors with each repositioning. A longer tape measure would be more appropriate.

items.stem: How much is 1 inch approximately equal to in centimetres ?
items.answer: (C) 2.54 cm The conversion factor given is that 1 inch equals

items.stem: If an object is in circular motion and its motion is also periodic, what does this imply?

options.label: A
options.text: It moves in a circle only once

options.label: B
options.text: It completes each circular path in a fixed interval of time

options.label: C
options.text: It changes its speed constantly while moving in a circle

options.label: D
options.text: It moves along a straight line after completing the circle

items.answer: (B) It completes each circular path in a fixed interval of time. Periodic motion means the motion repeats itself after a fixed time interval. If circular motion is periodic, it means the object repeatedly traverses the circular path, taking the same amount of time for each revolution.

items.stem: The movement of a piston in an engine up and down is an example of which type of motion?

options.label: B
options.text: Primarily linear motion (reciprocating) which can also be seen as oscillatory over its path

items.answer: (B) Primarily linear motion (reciprocating) which can also be seen as oscillatory over its path The piston moves back and forth in a straight line within the cylinder. This to-and-fro linear movement is a form of reciprocating motion, which is a type of oscillatory motion.

items.stem: What did Deepa’s mother ask the shopkeeper for to make a new uniform?
items.answer: Deepa’s mother asked for a two-metre cloth piece.

items.stem: Name one body part that was traditionally used for measuring length, as mentioned by Deepa’s friends.
items.answer: Handspan (or arm, foot, strides).

items.stem: What is the term for a quantity like hands pan when used for measurement?
items.answer: Hands pan, when used for measurement, is an example of a unit.

items.stem: Why do measurements of the same length differ when using body parts like hands pans?
items.answer: Measurements differ because body parts like hands pans are of different sizes for different people.

items.stem: Name one ancient Indian unit of length mentioned.
items.answer: Angula (or dhanusa, yojana).

items.stem: What is the full form of SI units?
items.answer: SI units stands for the International System of Units.

items.stem: What is the SI unit of length?
items.answer: The SI unit of length is metre.

items.stem: How many centimetres are there in one metre?
items.answer: There are 100 centimeters in one metre.

items.stem: How many millimeters are there in one centimeter?
items.answer: There are 10 millimeters in one centimeter.

items.stem: What larger unit of length is commonly used for measuring the distance between two cities?
items.answer: Kilometre (km) is used for measuring larger distances.

items.stem: What type of measuring device is suitable for measuring the girth of a tree?
items.answer: A flexible measuring tape is suitable for measuring the girth of a tree.

items.stem: How should your eye be positioned when reading a measurement on a scale to avoid errors?
items.answer: Your eye should be positioned directly above the mark being read on the scale.

items.stem: If a scale has a broken zero end, can it still be used for measurement?
items.answer: Yes, it can be used by starting from another full mark and subtracting that reading.

items.stem: How can the length of a curved line be measured using a thread?
items.answer: Place the thread along the curved line, then straighten the thread and measure its length with a scale.

items.stem: What is a fixed object or point called with respect to which distance is stated?
items.answer: It is called a reference point.

items.stem: When is an object said to be in motion?
items.answer: An object is said to be in motion if its position changes with respect to a reference point with time.

items.stem: What type of motion does an object exhibit when it moves along a straight line?
items.answer: It exhibits linear motion.

items.stem: What type of motion is the movement of an object along a circular path called?
items.answer: It is called circular motion.

items.stem: When an object moves to and fro about a fixed position, what is its motion called?
items.answer: Its motion is called oscillatory motion.

items.stem: What is motion called if an object repeats its path after a fixed interval of time?
items.answer: Such motion is called periodic motion.

items.stem: Why was there a need to develop standard units of measurement?
items.answer: Non-standard units like hands pans differ from person to person, leading to inconsistent measurements. Standard units ensure uniformity and avoid confusion in trade and communication.

items.stem: What are the two parts that express a measurement of length? Give an example.
items.answer: A measurement of length is expressed by a number and a unit. For example, if a table is 2 metres long, ‘2’ is the number and ‘metre’ is the unit.

items.stem: Mention two ancient Indian units of measurement and state where evidence of scales has been found.
items.answer: Two ancient Indian units are ‘angula’ (finger width) and ‘yojana’. Evidence of scales has been excavated from sites of the Harappan Civilization.

items.stem: Explain the relationship between metre, centimetre, and millimetre.
items.answer: One metre (m) equals 100 centimeters (cm). One centimetre (cm) equals 10 millimetres (mm). These are standard SI units for measuring length.

items.stem: What unit of length would be appropriate to measure the thickness of a coin? Why?
items.answer: Millimetre (mm) would be appropriate to measure the thickness of a coin because a coin is very thin, and millimetre is a small unit for precise measurement.

items.stem: Describe the correct way to place a scale when measuring the length of an object like a pencil.
items.answer: The scale should be placed in contact with the object, along its length, ensuring one end of the object aligns with a clear mark on the scale.

items.stem: If a scale’s zero mark is unclear, how can you accurately measure an object’s length starting from the 2 cm mark?
items.answer: Align one end of the object with the 2.0 cm mark. Read the mark at the other end. Subtract 2.0 cm from this reading to get the object’s length.

items.stem: How do visually challenged students measure lengths using a scale?
items.answer: Visually challenged students use scales with raised markings. They can feel these markings by touching them to determine the length.

items.stem: State two rules for writing units of length like metre or centimetre and their symbols.
items.answer: Symbols (m, cm) are written in lowercase and are not followed by ‘s’ for plural. A space is left between the number and the unit symbol.

items.stem: Why is a flexible measuring tape more suitable than a rigid metre scale for measuring a person’s chest?
items.answer: A flexible measuring tape can easily wrap around the curved surface of a person’s chest, providing an accurate measurement, which a rigid scale cannot do.

items.stem: What is a reference point? Why is it important when describing the position of an object?
items.answer: A reference point is a fixed object or location used for comparison. It is important because it provides a basis from which an object’s position or motion can be clearly described.

items.stem: How do kilometre stones on a highway help a traveller determine if they are getting closer to their destination?
items.answer: Kilometre stones indicate the remaining distance to a destination (reference point). Decreasing numbers on successive stones mean the traveller is getting closer.

items.stem: When is an object considered to be at rest? Give an example.
items.answer: An object is at rest if its position does not change with time with respect to a chosen reference point. For example, a book lying on a table.

items.stem: Can an object be in motion and at rest at the same time? Explain with an example.
items.answer: Yes, relative to different reference points. For example, passengers in a moving bus are at rest relative to the bus but in motion relative to a tree outside.

items.stem: Give two examples of objects exhibiting linear motion from your daily life.
items.answer: A car moving on a straight road and an apple falling from a tree are examples of objects exhibiting linear motion in daily life.

items.stem: Give two examples of objects exhibiting circular motion.
items.answer: The blades of a spinning fan and a stone whirled at the end of a string are examples of objects exhibiting circular motion.

items.stem: Give two examples of objects exhibiting oscillatory motion.
items.answer: The motion of a child on a swing and the to- and-fro movement of a pendulum in a clock are examples of oscillatory motion.

items.stem: How is periodic motion defined? Are circular and oscillatory motions periodic?
items.answer: Periodic motion is when an object repeats its path after a fixed interval of time. Yes, both circular and oscillatory motions are typically periodic in nature.

items.stem: A soldier marching in a parade exhibits what type of motion? Justify your answer.
items.answer: A soldier marching in a parade on a straight path exhibits linear motion because their movement is along a straight line from one point to another.

items.stem: The hands of a clock exhibit which type of motion?
items.answer: The hands of a clock primarily exhibit circular motion as they move along a circular path around the center of the clock face. They also exhibit periodic motion.

items.stem: Describe some non-standard units of measurement used in ancient times or even today for rough estimations. Why did these methods lead to the need for standard units like the metre?
items.answer: Anciently, body parts like hands pan, cubit (arm length), foot length, and strides were used. These are non-standard because their sizes vary from person to person. This variation caused confusion and inconsistency, especially in trade, necessitating the development of fixed, standard units like the metre for reliable and uniform measurements.

items.stem: Explain the SI system of units. What is the SI unit of length, and how is it subdivided into smaller units like centimeter and millimeter for convenience?
items.answer: The International System of Units (SI) is a globally adopted standard system for measurements. The SI unit of length is the metre (m). For convenience in measuring smaller lengths, one metre is divided into 100 equal parts called centimeters (cm), and one centimeter is further divided into 10 equal parts called millimeters (mm).

items.stem: List three important precautions one must take while measuring length using a standard scale to ensure accuracy. Explain why each precaution is necessary.
items.answer: 1. Place the scale correctly along the length of the object to avoid misreading.

items.stem: How can you measure the length of a curved path, for example, the boundary of an irregularly shaped garden pond? Describe the method in steps.
items.answer: To measure a curved path, one can use a thread. First, carefully lay the thread along the entire curved boundary of the pond, ensuring it follows the curves accurately. Mark the start and end points on the thread. Then, straighten the thread and measure its length between the marked points using a standard metre scale or measuring tape.

items.stem: Explain the concept of a ‘reference point’ in describing motion. Give an example to show how the choice of a reference point can change the description of an object’s state of motion.
items.answer: A reference point is a fixed location or object used to determine if another object’s position has changed. For instance, a person sitting in a moving train is at rest with respect to the train (reference point: train interior) but is in motion with respect to the tracks or trees outside (reference point: ground).

items.stem: Define linear, circular, and oscillatory motion. Provide one clear real-world example for each type, explaining why it fits the definition.
items.answer: Linear motion is movement along a straight line (e.g., a ball rolling straight on the floor). Circular motion is movement along a circular path (e.g., a point on a spinning top’s edge). Oscillatory motion is repetitive to-and-fro movement about a fixed position (e.g., a child on a swing).

items.stem: Imagine you are in a moving train with no windows, moving smoothly on a straight track. Can you tell if the train is moving or stationary without looking outside? Explain your reasoning. (Evaluating)
items.answer: If the train moves very smoothly at a constant speed on a straight track, it would be difficult to tell if it’s moving or stationary without an external reference point. This is because your body and objects inside would move with the train, feeling no change in motion relative to the train’s interior.

items.stem: Describe the correct procedure for reading a measurement from a scale, including the placement of the scale and the position of the eye. Why are these steps important?
items.answer: Place the scale in contact with the object, along its length, with the zero mark (or another full mark if zero is broken) aligned with one end. The eye should be directly above the point on the scale being read. These steps are crucial to avoid errors like parallax, ensuring the measurement is accurate.

items.stem: How are kilometre, metre, centimetre, and millimetre related to each other? Give an example of a length that would be best measured in each of these units.
items.answer: 1 km = 1000 m; 1 m = 100 cm; 1 cm = 10 mm. Distance between cities is best in km. Height of a door in metres. Length of a pencil in centimeters. Thickness of a wire in millimeters. Choosing appropriate units makes measurements practical and numbers manageable.

items.stem: What is periodic motion? Explain how both circular motion and oscillatory motion can be considered types of periodic motion, using examples.
items.answer: Periodic motion is any motion that repeats itself over a fixed interval of time. Circular motion, like the Earth revolving around the Sun, is periodic as it completes an orbit in a fixed time. Oscillatory motion, like a pendulum swinging, is also periodic as it repeats its to-and-fro movement regularly.

items.stem: A tailor is stitching a dress. He first measures the customer’s height using a measuring tape. Then, he measures the length of cloth required from a roll using a metal rod (metre scale). He needs to cut a curved neckline. (i) Which measuring device is more appropriate for measuring the customer’s chest circumference, and why? (ii) Why does the tailor use a rigid metal rod to measure cloth from a roll? (iii) How might the tailor measure the length of the curved neckline on the pattern paper?
items.answer: (i) A flexible measuring tape is more appropriate for measuring the chest circumference because it can easily conform to the curved shape of the body. (ii) The tailor uses a rigid metal rod (metre scale) to ensure the cloth is measured straight and accurately, without any stretching that a flexible tape might allow. (iii) The tailor might use a flexible measuring tape or a piece of thread, carefully laying it along the curved neckline on the pattern, and then measuring the thread’s length.

items.stem: A group of friends decided to measure the length of their classroom using their hands pans. Anil measured it as 20 hands pans, Sunita as 22 hands pans, and Ravi as 19 hands pans. They were confused by the different results. (i) Why did the friends get different measurements for the same classroom length? (ii) What type of unit is a ‘hands pan’ in this context? (iii) What should they use to get a consistent and accurate measurement of the classroom length?
items.answer: (i) They got different measurements because each person’s hands pan (the unit of measurement used) is of a different size. (ii) ‘Hands pan’ is a non-standard unit of measurement. (iii) They should use a standard measuring tool like a metre scale or a measuring tape to get a consistent and accurate measurement.

items.stem: An athlete is running on a 400 m circular track. She completes one lap. During her run, her coach observes her from a fixed point on the side of the track. (i) What is the distance covered by the athlete in one lap? (ii) What type of motion is the athlete primarily exhibiting while running on the track? (iii) Is the athlete in motion with respect to her coach? Explain.
items.answer: (i) The distance covered by the athlete in one lap is 400 m. (ii) The athlete is primarily exhibiting circular motion as she runs along the circular track. It is also periodic if she maintains pace. (iii) Yes, the athlete is in motion with respect to her coach because her position continuously changes relative to the coach (the reference point) as she runs.

items.stem: A child is playing on a swing in a park. The swing moves back and forth. Another child is sliding down a straight slide. A merry-go-round is also in motion nearby. (i) What type of motion does the child on the swing exhibit? (ii) What type of motion does the child sliding down the straight slide exhibit? (iii) If the merry-go-round is moving at a constant speed, its motion is circular. What other type of motion can it be classified as?
items.answer: (i) The child on the swing exhibits oscillatory motion. (ii) The child sliding down the straight slide exhibits linear motion. (iii) If the merry-go-round moves at a constant speed, its motion can also be classified as periodic motion because it repeats its path.

items.stem: To measure the length of a pencil, a student places it against a ruler. The tip of the pencil aligns with the 15 cm mark, and the eraser end aligns with the 3.5 cm mark.
